title: Dealing with ambiguity: context, probability, absurdity
summary: Japanese can look ambiguous, but three common-sense rules (context, probability and absurdity) settle almost every doubtful sentence.

blocks.text: Japanese has a name for being vague, and part of that is because of the **zero pronoun**: you cannot see the carriage. But the carriage is always there logically, and a hidden word works like English "it", which can mean anything and is only clear from context. Japanese is not magic. Speaker and listener fix doubts the same way English speakers do.
Three rules that settle most doubts

rows: What was said before points to the answer.
If two readings fit, take the likelier one.
Do not choose the silly reading unless the speaker makes the silliness clear.

blocks.text: Talking about lunch, a zero pronoun and a bare noun are enough.

blocks.en: I'll have udon. (said while choosing lunch)

blocks.text: English works the same way. "I saw a man on a hill with a telescope" could mean either of two things, but you take the likelier one.

blocks.en: I keep a cat. (not: a cat keeps me)

blocks.text: "I ate dinner with Sakura" and "I ate dinner with chopsticks" have the same structure, and nobody reads the second one as eating dinner together with chopsticks.

blocks.en: I'll have the fish. (at a restaurant, not: I am a fish)

blocks.text: Speakers expect listeners to use these rules, and languages are built around that. A speaker who wants a strange meaning has to say so clearly. The stranger the meaning, the more the speaker has to explain.
A famous overlap: potential and receptive

The ichidan **potential** (食べられる, "can eat") and the ichidan **receptive** (食べられる, "receive being eaten") look the same. Usually probability decides: nobody tells you "I got eaten" while standing there. With a pet mouse, however, only context can say.

blocks.en: The mouse could eat. / The mouse got eaten. (only context can tell)

blocks.text: Reading 1: the mouse was able to eat.

blocks.jp: この果物は子供でも食べられる。
blocks.en: Even a child can eat this fruit. (potential; the situation makes that clear)

blocks.text: A topic with は is not logical, but it still has to be **connected** to the comment after it. In the next sentence, the comment has a zero carriage, so the topic must be that carriage: the man is the one who bought bread.

blocks.jp: あの犬を連れた男は、駅の前でパンを買った。
blocks.en: The man with that dog bought bread in front of the station.

blocks.text: A reading in which the topic has nothing to do with the comment, like "speaking of a faraway galaxy, Sakura has a pimple", is possible only if the speaker makes the link clear. So the reader prefers a different structure. Context settles the rest:

items: The zero pronoun is always there, and context says who or what it is.
Ichidan **-られる** can be potential or receptive; use the situation to decide.
A real ambiguity can exist, as in any language; the speaker is responsible for making things clear.

questions.instruction: Which one is NOT one of the three rules?
questions.note: The three rules are context, probability and absurdity.

questions.instruction: You are choosing lunch together. What does this mean?
options: I am a bowl of noodles
questions.note: Context says we are ordering, so it means "I'll have soba".

questions.instruction: Which reading does probability prefer?
questions.note: If two readings fit, take the likelier one.
questions.en: My older brother has a car.

questions.instruction: In a café, someone says this. Which reading does absurdity rule out?
options: I am a cup of coffee
questions.note: Do not choose the silly reading unless the speaker makes it clear.

questions.instruction: What does the zero pronoun work like?
options: A hidden word like English "it", clear from context
questions.note: The carriage is always there logically, even when you cannot see it.

questions.instruction: Is 見られた potential or receptive here?
questions.note: The doer is marked with に and nobody boasts about being able to see, so it is receptive.
questions.en: My younger brother saw my letter.

questions.instruction: Is 食べられる potential or receptive here?
questions.prompt: あの子は一人でご飯が食べられる。
questions.note: A child who eats by himself fits probability: he can eat.
questions.en: That child can eat by himself.

questions.instruction: With no context, which reading is likelier?
options: The fish was able to eat
questions.note: Probability usually decides.

questions.instruction: Which sentence has a comment that connects to its は topic?
options: あの人は雨が降っている。
あの人は月が出ている。
questions.note: A は topic must connect to its comment: long legs belong to the person.

questions.instruction: Which reading does probability prefer?
questions.note: The likelier reading wins.

questions.instruction: What must a speaker do to get a strange meaning across?
questions.note: The speaker is responsible for making a strange reading clear.

questions.instruction: In a restaurant, you hear this. What does it most likely mean?
questions.note: Context (a restaurant) gives the comment a connection to the topic.

questions.instruction: The verb 見られる can be potential or receptive. Which of these is the same in both readings, so it cannot help you decide?
questions.note: The ichidan form is the same for both, so you need the other clues.

questions.instruction: Which rule says: use what was said before?
questions.note: Context points to the answer from earlier talk.

questions.instruction: Which rule says: do not choose the silly reading?
questions.note: Absurdity rules out meanings nobody would mean.

questions.instruction: Tap the topic that connects to the comment
questions.note: 弟は sets the topic; 足が長い describes him.
questions.en: My younger brother has long legs.

questions.instruction: Tap the receptive form
questions.note: 見られた with a に doer is receptive: it happened to me.
questions.en: My little sister saw my letter.

questions.instruction: Tap the potential form
questions.note: The situation says you can eat it, so 食べられる is potential.
questions.en: You can eat this fish raw.

questions.instruction: Build the sentence
questions.note: A は topic followed by a connected comment.

questions.instruction: Build the sentence
questions.prompt: He'll have coffee and I'll have tea.
questions.note: Context (ordering drinks) tells us 私はお茶だ means "I'll have tea", not "I am tea".
questions.en: He'll have coffee, and I'll have tea.

questions.instruction: Build the sentence
questions.prompt: My older sister saw my letter, and I was bothered.
questions.note: The doer takes に in a receptive sentence.
questions.en: My older sister saw my letter (and I was bothered).

questions.instruction: Is 食べられた potential or receptive?
questions.prompt: 昨日、一人で全部食べられた。
questions.note: Probability and context: someone alone eating it all is the doer.
questions.en: Yesterday I was able to eat it all by myself.

questions.instruction: In a noodle shop, what does this most likely mean?
options: That person is a bowl of ramen
questions.note: Context and absurdity point to the order.
